Mahbubur Rahman with Farrah Mahbub and Kalimullah Mazumder, Advocates — For the Petitioner.
Nikhilesh Dutta, Deputy Attorney-General with AKM Shafiuddin Deputy Attorney-General and Laykuzzaman, Assistant Attorney-General — For the State.
parties:
Major (Retd) M Khairuzzaman ------ Petitioners
Vs. 
State ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
By this application under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the accused-petitioner Major (Retd) M Khairuzzaman is seeking release on bail in GR Case No. 10598 of 1975 arising out of Lalbagh Police Station Case No. 11(11)75 under section 302 of the Penal Code. The case involves the killing of four national leaders on November 3, 1975 in the Dhaka Central Jail. 

 3. Further statements are that, the petitioner was suddenly arrested on 13th August, 1996 and was taken to Dhaka Central Jail where he was served with an order of detention dated 13-8-1996 under the Special Powers Act. The order of detention was declared illegal and without lawful authority by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3769 of 1996 but he could not be released on bail as he was later on shown arrested in Lalbagh Police Station Case No.11(11)75. The prayer for bail presented before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka was rejected on 23-10-1996. The prayer for bail before the learned Sessions Judge, Dhaka in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 1997 of 1996 was also rejected by the learned Sessions Judge on 27-11-1996. Another application for bail being Miscellaneous Case No. 2934 of 1977 before the learned Sessions Judge also stood rejected. The accused-petitioner, thereafter, moved an application before the High Court Division being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 2705 of 1997 under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Rule was issued on the said application but the same was discharged by a judgment dated November 11, 1997. The petitioner again moved an application for bail before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Dhaka on 26-1-1998 and the same was rejected on the same date and again an application for bail had been moved before the learned Sessions Judge, Dhaka and the said application was also rejected by the order dated 23-2-1998. The petitioner, thereafter, is presenting this application before this Court seeking his release on bail. 

 (ii) Since the investigation had not been completed immediately after the judgment of the High Court Division discharging the Rule in Miscellaneous Case No. 2705 of 1997, the accused-petitioner acquired a right to be enlarged on bail from this court. 

 (i) since the occurrence took place on 3rd November, 1975 and long 21 years passed after the occurrence, to collect evidences and materials necessary for holding proper investigation into the case, a considerable time is required and delay in the conclusion of the investigation cannot confer any right upon the accused-petitioner to be released on bail. 

 (iii) There is serious apprehension that the accused-petitioner, if enlarged on bail, shall abscond and leave the country and as he was an influential and powerful Army Officer, there is every possibility of his influencing the investigation and the proceeding of the case and also tampering with the evidences. The other accused persons are absconding and they are fugitives from justice. 

 8. The law applicable to the case of bail is provided under sections 496, 497 and 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The provisions of section 496 are attracted to an accused of bailable offence. Section 497, on the other hand, applies to an accused charged with non-bailable offence. It postulates that an accused charged with any non-bailable offence, when arrested or detained without warrant by an Officer-in-Charge of a police station or appears or brought before a court, he may be released on bail. Sub-section 2 prescribes that if it appears to an officer or a court, at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial, as the case may be, that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence and that there are sufficient grounds for a further inquiry into his guilt, the accused pending such inquiry be released on bail on execution of a bond for his appearance. 

 10. Under section 498 of the Code both the Court of Sessions and the High Court Division can exercise the discretionary power in enlarging any accused person on bail. The power to grant bail under section 498 is not additional to or independent of section 497 and the provisions contained in section 497 have to be kept in view while passing orders under section 498. The policy of the law in respect of bail to persons accused of non-bailable offences is laid down in section 497 and the same policy should be kept in view while considering the question of bail under section 498. Therefore, the power of the High Court Division to grant bail under section 498 is subservient and ancillary to section 497 which limits the power to grant bail in a case punishable with death or imprisonment for life. 

 11. It is well established that the grant of bail in a non-bailable offence is a concession and not a right. Before granting bail in a non-bailable case, the court, when the case is at the investigation stage, should take into consideration various matters such as the nature and seriousness of the offence, the character of the evidence in support of the prosecution, the severity of the punishment to which the accused may be subjected, the danger of the accused abusing the concession of bail by way of absconding and tampering with the evidence, the larger interest of the public or the State, whether the grant of bail would thwart the course of justice and similar other considerations. None of the above considerations is a sufficient reason for the grant of bail but any one of those considerations can be a good ground for the refusal of bail. Putting the whole thing succinctly, the only objective that a Court dealing with an application for bail must keep in view is that in no case there be any impediment in the progress of investigation/trial. 

 12. The accused-petitioner had been arrested in Lalbagh Police Station Case No.11(11)75 for his alleged involvement in the killing of four National leaders namely, Mr Syed Nazrul Islam, MrTajuddin Ahmed , Mr Captain (Rtd) Monsur Ali and Mr AHM Quamruzzaman. Late Mr Syed Nazrul Islam was the Acting President of the temporary Government at Mujibnagar and the Vice-President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Late Mr Tajuddin Ahmed was the Prime Minister of the said temporary Government at Mujibnagar and the Finance Minister of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Late Mr Captain (Rtd) Mansur Ali was the Finance Minister of the temporary Government and the Prime Minister of the Republic and Late Mr AHM Quamruzzaman was the Home Minister of the temporary Government and the Relief and Rehabilitation Minister of the Republic. The four national leaders were the great heroes and organisers of the glorious Liberation Movement of Bangladesh of 1971 against the Pakistan Occupation Forces. In the night following November 2, 1975 (3-11-1975) the four national leaders were brutally killed inside the Dhaka Central Jail. It appears that the Jail Authority lodged a First Information Report with Lalbagh Police Station which was registered as Lalbagh Police Station Case No. 11(11)75 dated 4-11-1975. The said case was pending in the Lalbagh Police Station and no further steps were taken so far and only in the middle part of the year 1996, the proceeding/investigation of the said Lalbagh case had started. The Jail murder occurrence took place on November 3, 1975, that is 21 years ago. The collection of evidences and materials after a period of long 21 years becomes a difficult task and it is quite natural that some time will be consumed in holding proper investigation into the case and in bringing the truth to light. Section 167 (5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure enjoins that if investigation is not concluded within 120 days from the date of receipt of the information relating to the commission of the offence, the court, if satisfied, can release the accused on bail. But the accused cannot claim the privilege of bail as a matter of right. In the face of peculiar circumstances, delay in completion of investigation of the case is no ground to release the accused-petitioner on bail. 

 13. It is seen from various annexures and materials on record placed before this court that prayer for bail of the accused-petitioner had been submitted before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka who was pleased to reject the same by his order dated 23-10-96. The accused petitioner, thereafter, moved an application for bail being numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 1777 of 1996 before the learned Sessions Judge, Dhaka who also rejected the said prayer on 27-11-1996. In rejecting the bail prayer the Learned Sessions Judge was of the view that the prosecution story gets support from the statement recorded by the accused-petitioner under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. From the order dated 27-11-1996 it is manifested that the accused petitioner made a statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure with respect to the occurrence of November 3, 1975. In this application for bail it is stated that he made a statement before the police about his whereabouts. Another application for bail being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 2034 of 1997 had been filed before the Sessions Judge, Dhaka and the said application for bail was also rejected by the order dated 16-6-1997. The accused-petitioner then moved an application under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the High Court Division and the said application was registered as Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 2705 of 1997. Rule issued on the said application was ultimately discharged by a Division Bench of this Court by the judgment dated November 19, 1997. In discharging the Rule the said Division Bench recorded thus: "Considering the fact that four national leaders of this country were killed in the jail when the present petitioner was serving in the Army and since it is submitted by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that there were materials against the petitioner and others for which very soon the charge-sheet will be submitted in the case and since there is every chance of ascension and influencing the proceeding of the case, we are of the view that this is not a fit case where we should exercise our discretion in granting bail at this stage." The accused-petitioner appeared not to have felt aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment of the High Court Division and did not ventilate his grievance before the Appellate Division by presenting a leave petition. The rejection of bail to the accused petitioner by the High Court Division could not deter him from moving any further application for bail before the Courts below. Another application for bail was moved before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate on 26-1-1998 and the said application also stood rejected. The accused-petitioner, thereafter, moved another application for bail on 19-2-98 before the Sessions Judge, Dhaka. The bail matter was heard on 23-2-98 by the learned Additional Sessions Judge who was pleased to reject the same. The accused petitioner again presented this application under section 498 of the Criminal Procedure Code before this court praying for bail. 

 14. True it is that section 167(5) provides for releasing an accused on bail if the court is satisfied as to releasing him on bail but in the case in our hand neither the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate nor the Sessions Judge, Dhaka was satisfied in the matter of enlarging the accused petitioner on bail keeping in view the serious nature of offence, the statement recorded by the accused-petitioner under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and another circumstances of the case. The learned Additional Sessions Judge in rejecting the application for bail by his order dated 23-2-1998 considered the rejection of bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Case Nos. 1777 of 1996 and 2034 of 1997 of the Court of Sessions and also of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 2705 of 1997 by the High Court Division. The order dated 23-2-1998 does not appear to have suffered from any illegality. Satisfaction is also wanting on the part of this Court in releasing the accused-petitioner on bail. 

 15. Turning now to the serious objection rose from the side of the State that there is every chance of the accused-petitioner''s ascension and destroying the evidence against himself if he is released on bail. In an application for bail of an accused person for an alleged offence of commission of murder, the most important circumstance which a court considers is the possibility that an accused person or an accused suspected may abscond and destroy the evidence against him and defeat the ends justice. The seriousness and gravity of the offence and the severity of punishment are very probable factors which may tempt an accused or suspected accused to escape the clutches of law. Again there is also temptation of destroying the evidence and materials against him. The whole object of arrest and detention of an accused person is obviously to secure his appearance to abide the sentence of law. The accused petitioner was arrested in connection with Lalbagh Police Station Case No. 11(11) 75 under section 302 of the Penal Code. Admittedly, he was an Army Officer on November 3, 1975 and he served in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for about 20 years. He served in different Embassies in different countries of the world and he is supposed to have good contacts with the people of those countries where he served and stayed as a diplomat. The accused-petitioner being an accused or suspected in a case of brutal killing of four national leaders inside Dhaka Central Jail where the punishment is death or life imprisonment, may abscond and leave the country to take shelter in those countries where he stayed as diplomat and also may not resist temptation of destroying evidences against him. In this context the point pressed from the side of the State that the other accused persons are absconding and they are fugitives from justice may not be also overlooked in considering the bail matter of the accused-petitioner. So, the objection raised from the side of the State cannot be blown away. It is true that the investigation has not been completed within 19 months of the arrest of the accused-petitioner yet it will not be safe to release the accused petitioner on bail till the completion of the investigation and thereafter. 

 16. Regard being had to the facts, circumstances, materials on record, nature and seriousness of the offence, the larger interests of the public and the State and similar other considerations and also keeping in view the various considerations of granting bail in non-bailable offence, the instant case hardly presents features warranting grant of bail to the accused-petitioner. We are not at all inclined to exercise the discretionary power under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to release the accused-petitioner on bail.
